claims.text: Selective oxidation of element X governs formation and persistence of the protective oxide layer in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Al- or Si-containing variants form oxides with high chemical stability.
Oxides derived from Al or Si have low lattice mismatch with the underlying CrFeCoNiX substrate.
High oxide stability and low oxide–substrate lattice mismatch cause a continuous, adherent oxide layer to form.
The Mn-containing alloy forms an oxide scale with higher lattice misfit and stress than the Al- or Si-containing alloys.
Higher oxide–substrate lattice misfit generates stress that promotes oxide cracking or spallation.
Oxide-layer coherence depends on lattice and chemical compatibility between the X-derived oxide and the alloy substrate.
Selective oxidation of X produces an X-derived oxide.
Low lattice mismatch and minimal growth-induced stress allow the oxide to act as a stable, coherent diffusion barrier.
CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi are predicted to form thin, continuous, adherent oxide layers under prolonged exposure above 900 °C.
The oxide layers on the Al- and Si-containing alloys will resist cracking and spallation.
CrFeCoNiMn is predicted to develop thicker and less coherent oxide scales than the Al- or Si-containing variants.
The oxide scales on CrFeCoNiMn will be more prone to cracking or spallation.
The proposed mechanism applies to single- or multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions exposed above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
Changes in composition other than X, phase structure, or exposure conditions may alter the oxidation behavior.
Prior observations support a role for oxide–substrate lattice coherence in oxide-scale stability.
